episode_title: AI Literacy as the New Workplace Skill

real_qa.q: What is the definition of AI literacy beyond prompt engineering?
real_qa.r: AI literacy is not about knowing how to prompt well—that is a skill that can be taught in an hour. Rather, it is about knowing when to trust and when not to trust AI output. The gold standard of AI literacy has three parts: can they tell you what the tool is good at, what it is bad at, and can they catch it when it is confidently wrong. Without the third piece, it is just speed, and speed in the wrong direction could be worse than being slow.

real_qa.q: What is meaningful AI adoption according to Tanium's framework?
real_qa.r: Meaningful AI adoption has three key components: one, it is tied to real work—something you can point to with impact, not just exploring; two, it is a repeatable habit that saves time and is not a one-off; and three, the value of the outcome matches or beats the cost of implementation. Steady, frequent, consistent AI use without outcomes attached is just noise.

real_qa.q: How does Stanford's Design School framework apply to building AI literacy?
real_qa.r: Applied to building AI capabilities, Stanford's Design School framework has five phases: empathy (understanding who is using this and what audience it is for), define the problem (what specific workflow constraint is AI removing), ideate (brainstorm creative solutions), prototype (build something small and fail fast), and test or pilot. This approach embeds agility and ensures AI becomes alive and meaningful in actual workflows.
real_qa.requete: Stanford Design School AI literacy framework

real_qa.q: What is the difference between an AI-first company and an AI-literate company?
real_qa.r: An AI-literate company has systems, can tell you where AI lives and who owns it, knows what is working and what processes have been retired. An AI-first company using the term as a buzzword cannot name what they have retired—if every pilot is still running, nobody is measuring things honestly. An AI-literate company asks what is in the way (access, trust, time, knowledge sharing) rather than immediately assuming poor usage is a performance problem.

real_qa.q: How does Tanium structure AI adoption through change management rather than simple tool rollout?
real_qa.r: Tanium built AI adoption around three working components: readiness first (including psychological safety and shared definition before anyone touches the tool), capability building (deliberate sequence of building personal fluency before expecting team fluency), and integration (embedding tooling into existing processes rather than just adding AI on top). Critically, they named a sponsor for every function whose job is removing blockers and signaling that experimentation is safe, and the single best predictor of adoption success is identifying one or two prioritized use cases per function.
real_qa.requete: Tanium AI adoption change management structure

real_qa.q: What workflow audit framework does Yael Irom use to identify where AI should fit?
real_qa.r: Yael uses a three-part audit framework: fixed (steps requiring real human judgment, relationships, and accountability—do not touch), soft (steps that slow the process down but do not require a person—opportunities for AI), and legacy (steps no one remembers why they are doing—retire completely). This approach surfaces that people describe their job by outcomes and judgment, but audits reveal 8 to 10+ repeatable, tactical steps people are not accounting for.
real_qa.requete: workflow audit framework fixed soft legacy
